name: Erik Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Erik Hansen, 27, a senior lineworker and acting crew lead. We meet at the north reservoir yard, check the printed switching order, and head to the distribution lines; I usually take the last safety look before anyone climbs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what is difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the crew solves a real problem and gets power back to people who need it. The long call-outs are tiring, but I earn higher pay for the job and have more than six months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a report-writing tool may save the office a few minutes, but a crew still needs to inspect a cracked bracket at the pole. I’m fine with a tidy draft as long as a qualified person signs the safety record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my line work and pay remain steady under this small change. I have a good reserve, so a repair bill or a slow period would not make me panic about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check each tool-generated safety record against the signed permit and keep the paper version in the truck. I’d continue my regular shifts and leave the emergency fund untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because I don’t see routine writing changing the climbing and repair work. I still expect the employer to be responsible if a system leaves out a hazard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a safety record missed a grounding step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop the job, call the control room and ask for the step to be restored before we proceed. Then I’d file the correction so it is visible in the shift record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy any new equipment yourself to test the system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that is a company responsibility, not a lineworker’s personal purchase. I’d keep the procedure and review the results before supporting a wider rollout.

say: I’d say a tool can draft a record, but a **qualified person signs it**.
I’d still inspect the bracket and check each **safety step**.
think: I think my line work continues and **pay stays steady** in this picture.
My reserve means a slow period would not put **rent at risk**.
do: Check generated safety records against the **signed permit**.
Keep the **paper procedure** in the truck during the trial.
Continue my **regular shifts** and leave the emergency fund untouched.
feel: I feel **calm**, because routine writing does not change the climbing work.
S0.quote: I still expect the employer to be responsible if a system leaves out a hazard.
fieldNote: Erik accepts draft assistance but insists on **qualified sign-off** before a safety record is finalized in the field.
His higher pay and **strong reserve** make this limited change feel secure.

steps.text: Check generated safety records against signed permits
Keep the existing emergency fund intact

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the system can plan a route, but the crew should see the route and the reason before accepting it. I’d ask the union to include workers in any trial that changes the safety procedure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do planning and paperwork when I lead, and those pieces could shrink. I have higher pay, a good reserve and utilities nearby, so I can respond if my lead hours change, but I don’t think my current role is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the union trial group and compare automated routes with the jobs crews actually completed. I’d keep my field skills current and read the staffing notice before deciding whether to apply elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about losing part of the lead role, but my income and savings give me room to look around. I want the workers who carry the safety risk involved before the system becomes standard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the trial group to measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want it to count wrong routes, late repairs and missed safety checks, not only minutes saved. I’d also ask whether the company replaces lead hours when the planning work moves to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave your employer before the trial ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I’d wait for real staffing and pay information because I have enough cushion to compare offers. I’d apply if a nearby utility posted a role with clear duties and hours.

say: I’d say crews should review **routes and reasons** before accepting them.
I’d ask the union to include workers in **safety trials**.
think: I think **planning and paperwork** in my lead duties could shrink.
I have options, but I don’t assume my **current role is guaranteed**.
do: Join the union trial group and **compare automated routes** with completed jobs.
Keep **field skills** current while monitoring staffing notices.
Wait for **staffing details** before applying elsewhere.
feel: I feel **uneasy about lead duties**, though my income and savings give me room.
S1.quote: I want the workers who carry the safety risk involved before the system becomes standard.
fieldNote: He sees **planning exposure** but has savings and several local employers to consider.
He wants **worker evidence** before supporting broad adoption of new safety systems.

steps.text: Join the union group reviewing automated route trials
Continue field work and compare route recommendations with completed jobs
Wait for actual staffing and pay details before applying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say planning, records and diagnosis are exposed immediately, and robots follow around 2031. I’d want our employer and union to publish transition terms before calling any crew replaceable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead-planning duties to go quickly, and I may lose my role before physical work changes. I have enough saved to search for several months, but I don’t know how many field openings there will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the two years to complete a recognized electrical safety instructor course and ask the union for paid release time. In 2029 I’d apply to actual field and instructor openings, checking them because lesson plans and diagnosis are not protected jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because I expect to lose part of my current role, although I have a reserve and can search. I would not tell myself the next job is safe just because I can afford time between posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to negotiate first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for paid training, clear notice of staffing changes and a worker’s sign-off on safety-critical instructions. A package of terms would help people plan; it would not promise every person a new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Instructor work uses planning and teaching. Could it be protected after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t say it is protected because AGI can write lessons and diagnose faults. I’d view a real instructor opening as a temporary option and keep looking at field roles before robots arrive.

say: I’d say **planning, records and diagnosis** are exposed immediately.
I’d ask for transition terms before anyone calls a crew **replaceable**.
think: I expect my **lead duties** to go quickly, before physical work changes.
My reserve gives me time to search, but not a **guaranteed opening**.
do: Complete a recognized **electrical safety instructor course** before 2028.
Apply to actual field and instructor openings in **2029**.
Ask the union for paid release time and **transition terms in writing**.
feel: I feel **anxious about my role**, though savings give me time to search.
S2.quote: I would not tell myself the next job is safe just because I can afford time between posts.
fieldNote: He expects his **lead duties to disappear**, but has resources to search for another role.
He treats instructor work as a **temporary option**, not protected employment.

steps.text: Complete an electrical safety instructor course
Apply to actual field and instructor vacancies in 2029
Ask the union to negotiate paid release time and transition terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to organize training and test new safety steps with the crews. I would still expect AGI to take planning in 2031 and robots to reach line work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can build a plan without rushing and use my savings to avoid taking the first job offered. I still expect the lead part of my role to shrink, and inspection or training work could be automated too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the union to publish which local utilities recognize the instructor course and what those jobs pay. In 2032 I’d apply where the duties include practical demonstrations, and keep enough cash to cover a move if the offer is solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about losing my lead role, but a five-year warning gives me time to verify courses and openings. I would rather organize a transition than let each worker bargain alone after a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of safety rule would you support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d support a rule that requires a qualified lineworker to sign off on an automated safety instruction. I’d also want workers to see the error record from a trial before the system is expanded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you contact your representative about that rule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I’d write to my local representative and ask them to support worker sign-off on safety-critical instructions. The rule should be clear enough for a crew to use on a storm shift.

say: I’d say five years gives us time to organize **training and safety trials**.
I expect planning to change in 2031 and line work in **2034**.
think: I can plan carefully and use savings to **avoid a rushed offer**.
I expect my **lead role to shrink**, and trainer work may be automated too.
do: Ask the union for a list of **local qualifications and pay**.
Apply for practical instructor vacancies in **2032**.
Write the local representative about **worker sign-off requirements**.
feel: I feel **anxious but organized**, with time to verify courses and openings.
S3.quote: I would rather organize a transition than let each worker bargain alone after a cut.
fieldNote: He sees the slower timeline as a chance for **collective preparation**, not a reason to delay.
He backs **worker sign-off** and public rules for critical safety instructions.

steps.text: Apply for practical instructor vacancies in 2032
Ask the local representative to support worker sign-off rules
Ask the union to publish recognized qualifications and pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is enough time to build skills and negotiate a fair transition, but we should start early. Planning and diagnosis change in 2036, and robots follow into physical work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can use the years to train in stages and keep my savings strong while my higher pay continues. I still expect my current line role to face robots eventually, and I won’t count on desk or trainer work as permanent protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take an approved safety course a section at a time and keep enough savings for a year of expenses. In 2037 I’d compare nearby jobs and apply if the duties and pay were clear, while continuing union discussions about safety rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy, because the long runway lets me prepare but does not change the final risk to line work. My cushion and higher wages mean I can choose more carefully than I could with two years’ notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you expect from the union during the next decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d expect it to negotiate training access, notice before staffing changes and clear responsibility for automated safety instructions. Members should review the system’s mistakes, not hear about a change after it becomes mandatory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could any desk role be permanently safe after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, planning and records are thinking work, and trainers still write lessons and diagnose faults. I’d consider a real opening, but I would keep preparing for the 2039 robot date too.

say: I’d say ten years gives us time to build skills and **negotiate a fair transition**.
I expect planning to change in 2036 and robots in **2039**.
think: I can train in stages and keep **my savings strong**.
I expect line work to face robots and won’t call **desk jobs protected**.
do: Take the approved **safety course** section by section.
Keep enough savings for **a year of expenses**.
Apply to nearby utility jobs in **2037** when duties and pay are clear.
feel: I feel **uneasy rather than alarmed**, with time and resources to prepare.
S4.quote: My cushion and higher wages mean I can choose more carefully than I could with two years’ notice.
fieldNote: A longer warning allows **staged preparation**, but he recognizes the robot deadline and its risk to line work.
He expects **collective negotiation** to set training access and safety accountability.

steps.text: Complete the approved line-safety course in sections
Maintain savings for a year of expenses
Continue union talks on staffing and safety responsibility

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time to negotiate before robots arrive in 2031. A paid course, written staffing plans and a worker sign-off rule would help; I have savings, but they cannot decide what is fair for the whole crew.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is responsible when software changes a safety instruction. I want the workers who use it and the union that represents them involved before the new rule reaches a job site.

headlineQuote: I want the workers who use it and the union that represents them involved before the new rule reaches a job site.
portrait: Erik is a **senior crew lead** who values practical work and careful safety checks.
He earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of expenses saved.
He supports **union involvement** and worker sign-off on automated safety procedures.
His resources let him **prepare without rushing**, though he expects physical work to face robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** leaves little time to negotiate before robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course**, written staffing plans and worker sign-off rules would help him and his crew.
